Systemd Integration

Abbreviations used on this page (TSDB, WAL, TTL, HWM, XPUB, ZMQ, SQLite, JSON, CLI, API, RSS, fd, PEP, CORS, OBS...) are defined in the Abbreviations & jargon section.

Systemd is the tool most Linux computers use to start programs in the background and keep them running. Running sqtseries as a systemd service gives it three things automatically: it starts when you boot the computer, it restarts if it crashes, and its logs are collected in one place (journald). sqtseries install writes a pre-hardened unit file and enables + starts it; sqtseries uninstall removes it.

Install

# per-user service (no root)
sqtseries install

# system-wide (root) — run as a dedicated user in production
sudo sqtseries install --system

install does three things: writes the unit file, runs systemctl --user daemon-reload (or plain daemon-reload for --system), and runs systemctl [--user] enable --now sqtseries (start now + start on boot). It uses the Python interpreter of the sqtseries command you ran (its sys.executable), so the unit starts the same Python that installed it.

There is no root check in the code: --system simply targets /etc/systemd/system, so without root the write fails with a permission error — run it under sudo.

User vs system unit

User unit (default)System unit (--system)
Location~/.config/systemd/user/sqtseries.service/etc/systemd/system/sqtseries.service
Controlsystemctl --user ... (or journalctl --user ...)sudo systemctl ... (or journalctl ...)
Runs asyour user, in your sessionthe installing user (auto-detected into User= with full home access, so the database stays under their $HOME); root only when no installing user is detected — or use the dedicated user below
Boot startafter you log in (needs loginctl enable-linger $USER to survive logout)on boot, independent of any login

The generated unit

Rendered with the database at its default location, for a per-user install with a config file (lines shown are the exact template):

[Unit]
Description=sqtseries time-series database
After=network.target
StartLimitIntervalSec=60
StartLimitBurst=3

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/home/user/.venv/bin/python -m sqtseries --config /home/user/sqtseries.toml run
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
SyslogIdentifier=sqtseries

# Security hardening
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=read-only
ReadWritePaths=/home/user/.sqtseries/data /home/user/.sqtseries/backups

# Environment
Environment=LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libjemalloc.so.2
Environment=SQT_SERIES_DATABASE__PATH=/home/user/.sqtseries/data/db.sqlite
Environment=SQT_SERIES_LOGGING__LEVEL=INFO

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

Field by field:

DirectiveValuePurpose
[Unit] Afternetwork.targetStart once the network stack is up (the service binds local sockets).
StartLimitIntervalSec / StartLimitBurst60 / 3Refuse to start more than 3 times within 60 s — breaks crash loops (e.g. a persistent port conflict).
Typesimplesqtseries stays in the foreground and is the main process.
ExecStart<python> -m sqtseries [--config <path>] runThe same command the CLI runs. --config appears only when you installed with one.
Restarton-failureRestart only when the process exits abnormally (non-zero, or killed by a signal).
RestartSec5Wait 5 s between restarts.
StandardOutput / StandardErrorjournalAll logs go to journald, nothing is written to files.
SyslogIdentifiersqtseriesTag for journalctl -u sqtseries.
NoNewPrivilegestrueCannot gain new privileges (setuid etc.).
ProtectSystemstrictThe whole filesystem is read-only for the service.
ProtectHomeread-only~ is readable but not writable.
ReadWritePathsdatabase parent dir + backup.path dirThe only places the service may write: its SQLite file lives in the first, backups written by sqtseries backup go to the second.
Environment=LD_PRELOADpath of libjemalloc.so.2 when present, otherwise omittedUses the jemalloc allocator when the machine has it (returns freed memory faster under sustained load); plain default allocator otherwise. The service runs correctly either way.
Environment=SQT_SERIES_DATABASE__PATHresolved database.pathKeeps the service pointed at the same database the CLI resolves to (including any --db you used when installing).
Environment=SQT_SERIES_LOGGING__LEVELINFOStable log level for the journal.
WantedBydefault.targetStart (and auto-start) with the default target, i.e. normal boot.

Production layout (/opt)

A production install (make deploy or cd dist && sudo make install) lays out exactly these paths — verified on this machine, all readable by the installing user:

PathWhat it is
/opt/sqtseriesproduction venv (bin/python3, bin/sqtseries)
/opt/sqtseries/config.tomlservice config (installed from the template on first install; never overwritten)
/usr/local/bin/sqtseriessymlink to the production console script
~/.sqtseries/data/db.sqlitedefault database (owned by you, writable)
~/.sqtseries/backups/default snapshot directory
/etc/systemd/system/sqtseries.servicesystem unit (only with --system)
~/.config/systemd/user/sqtseries.serviceuser unit (default install)

Custom ports and settings (--config)

Install with a config file and the file's path is embedded in ExecStart, so the service boots with exactly the ports and settings you configured. As with every command, --config is a global flag and must come before the subcommand:

sqtseries --config config.toml install            # per-user
sudo sqtseries --config config.toml install --system

From then on the unit runs python -m sqtseries --config config.toml run. Change the config and restart the unit to apply the new values. --db works the same way when installing without a config: the database path is embedded via SQT_SERIES_DATABASE__PATH and ReadWritePaths.

Management commands

Manage the service with systemctl (and inspect it with the sqtseries CLI). There is no sqtseries enable/disable/restart/logs command — those are systemctl/journalctl:

systemctl --user status sqtseries
systemctl --user restart sqtseries
systemctl --user stop sqtseries
systemctl --user enable sqtseries        # start on boot
systemctl --user disable sqtseries       # stop auto-start

# system service
sudo systemctl status sqtseries
sudo systemctl restart sqtseries

Status & logs

sqtseries status            # reads runtime: pid, ports, db
journalctl --user -u sqtseries -f        # follow logs
journalctl --user -u sqtseries -n 100    # last 100 lines
journalctl --user -u sqtseries --since today
# system service: journalctl -u sqtseries -f

Logs go to journald, not a file. On a headless server, enable lingering so the user service survives logout:

loginctl enable-linger $USER

Restart semantics and graceful shutdown

Restart=on-failure only restarts when the process exits abnormally. sqtseries handles SIGTERM and SIGINT with a graceful shutdown — it drains in-flight work, checkpoints the WAL, removes its runtime file, and exits 0. A deliberate systemctl stop, sqtseries stop or Ctrl-C therefore does not trip Restart. Only genuine failures (crash, non-zero exit) trigger a restart, and the StartLimitIntervalSec 60 + StartLimitBurst 3 guard stops a crash loop from hammering the machine. Clean shutdowns are logged as "shutting down" / "shutdown complete" in the journal.

System service as a dedicated user

For production, run the system unit under its own user with the database in a service-owned directory:

sudo useradd -r -s /bin/false sqtseries
sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/sqtseries /var/backups/sqtseries \
&& sudo chown -R sqtseries:sqtseries /var/lib/sqtseries /var/backups/sqtseries

# config.toml with the data/backup locations and any custom ports
cat > /etc/sqtseries/config.toml <<'EOF'
[database]
path = "/var/lib/sqtseries/db.sqlite"

[backup]
path = "/var/backups/sqtseries/"

# custom ports, retention, etc. go here too
EOF

sudo sqtseries --config /etc/sqtseries/config.toml install --system

Then edit /etc/systemd/system/sqtseries.service to set User=sqtseries (auto-detection picks the installing user, so point it at the dedicated one by hand) with a matching ReadWritePaths, then reload:

# add to [Service]:
#   User=sqtseries
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart sqtseries

Without the hand edit, a system install serves the installing user's database (auto-detected User=); after it, the service runs with those permissions (and NoNewPrivileges / ProtectSystem=strict keep the exposure small).

Uninstall

sqtseries uninstall          # stop + disable + remove the unit (user)
sudo sqtseries uninstall --system

uninstall runs systemctl [--user] disable --now sqtseries and removes the unit file. Uninstalling the unit does not delete your data. To remove the package and data too, see the the README (CLI reference).
